definition.text: A coral reef is an underwater ecosystem built by reef-building corals, colonies of tiny animals called polyps held together by calcium carbonate.

facts.text: Sometimes called rainforests of the sea, shallow coral reefs are among Earth's most diverse ecosystems.
Reefs cover less than 0.1% of the ocean, about half the area of France, yet house at least 25% of all marine species.
Coral reefs are estimated to cover 284,300 km2, 91.9% of it in the Indo-Pacific region.
Most reefs grow best in warm, shallow, clear, sunny and agitated water, even though that water holds few nutrients.
Over 4,000 species of fish live on coral reefs.
Fringing reefs protect nearby mangroves and seagrass meadows from strong currents and waves.
Shallow tropical coral reefs have declined by 50% since 1950.
Coral reefs first appeared 485 million years ago, but most living reefs are less than 10,000 years old.

definition.text: Coral reefs are classed by shape and setting, classically as fringing reefs, barrier reefs and atolls, with platform reefs often added.

facts.text: A fringing reef is attached to the shore or separated from it by a narrow, shallow channel.
A barrier reef is separated from the shore by a deep channel or lagoon.
An atoll is a roughly circular reef surrounding a lagoon with no central island, usually grown from a fringing reef around a volcanic island.
Platform reefs grow wherever the seabed rises near enough to the surface for reef-building corals.

definition.text: Coral polyps cannot photosynthesize themselves but live in partnership with tiny algae, called zooxanthellae, inside their tissues.

facts.text: The algae feed the polyp with sugars such as glucose, glycerol and amino acids.
Stressed corals expel these colourful algae, a response called bleaching.

title: Coral reef ecosystem services

definition.text: Coral reefs give people valuable services, chiefly tourism, fisheries and protection of coastlines.

facts.text: About 500 million people benefit from coral reef ecosystem services.
The global economic value of coral reefs has been estimated at between US$29.8 billion and $375 billion per year.
Destroying one square kilometre of reef was estimated to cost between $137,000 and $1,200,000 over 25 years.
About six million tons of fish are taken from reefs each year; a well-managed reef yields on average 15 tons of seafood per square kilometre a year.
Southeast Asia's reef fisheries alone yield about $2.4 billion in seafood a year.
The World Resources Institute built tools to value reef tourism, shoreline protection and fisheries to support coastal policy.
A Belize study valued reef and mangrove services at $395–559 million a year; Bermuda's reefs were valued at $722 million a year on average.

contested_note: Estimates of the annual global value of coral reefs differ by orders of magnitude between studies.

conflicts.note: Different study and year; method likely differs.

definition.text: Coral reefs protect coastlines by absorbing wave energy before it reaches the shore.

facts.text: Reefs can cut wave energy by 97%, helping prevent deaths and property damage; many small islands would not exist without them.
Reefs can damp waves as well as or better than artificial breakwaters, and restoring reefs is much cheaper than building breakwaters in the tropics.
About 197 million people living below 10 m elevation and within 50 km of a reef may get risk reduction from reefs.
Without the top meter of reefs, expected flood damage would double and costs from frequent storms would triple.
For 100-year storms, flood damage would rise by 91% to $US 272 billion without that top meter.

definition.text: Coral reefs are threatened by nutrient pollution, warming and acidifying oceans, overfishing and destructive land and sea uses.

facts.text: Coral reefs worldwide declined 14% from 2009 to 2018.
Local threats include coral mining, bottom trawling, blast fishing, overfishing and marine pollution, which persist where regulation is weak.
Greenhouse gas emissions warm the sea and raise sea level, causing widespread bleaching and loss of coral cover.
Ocean acidification slows coral calcification and speeds dissolution, though corals can partly adjust.
Overfishing and excess nutrients from land let algae outcompete and kill coral.
70–90% of today's warm-water coral reefs will disappear even if warming is kept to 1.5 °C.

title: Coral bleaching

definition.text: Coral bleaching is the stress response in which corals expel the colourful symbiotic algae living in their tissues.

facts.text: Rising sea temperatures from greenhouse gas emissions cause widespread bleaching.
El Niño events every 4–7 years bleach heat-sensitive reefs, with especially widespread bleaching in 1998 and 2010.
The Status of Coral Reefs of the World 2025 report found recovery time between warming events has shrunk from about a decade to five or six years in many regions.
Corals with some algal types (Clade A or D) resist heat bleaching better than those with Clade C, and some reefs become more resistant after a severe event.

title: Coral reef protection

definition.text: Coral reefs are protected mainly through marine protected areas and limits on fishing, pollution and coastal development.

facts.text: Marine protected areas aim at responsible fishery management and habitat protection, and can also serve restoration, biodiversity and economic goals.
Their effectiveness is still debated: some studied sites showed no difference from unprotected areas, and some caused local conflict.
Some protected areas provide local revenue roughly equal to what people would have earned without controls.
Protected areas seem able to protect reefs, but only with clear management and enough money.
Healthier Caribbean reefs have large parrotfish populations, found in countries that protect parrotfish and ban fish trapping and spearfishing.
Protecting networks of diverse, healthy reefs preserves the genetic diversity corals need to adapt to new climates.

contested_note: The sources say the effectiveness of marine protected areas for coral reefs is still debated.

definition.text: Coral farming, or coral gardening, grows coral fragments in nurseries and then replants them on damaged reefs.

facts.text: Gardening skips the early growth stages when young corals are most likely to die.
It relies on corals' natural ability to keep growing from fragments that anchor to new surfaces.
Coral nurseries became the most widespread and arguably most effective restoration method, largely replacing transplanting whole colonies.
Coral restoration grew because of unprecedented reef die-offs worldwide.

definition.text: A floodplain is the land beside a river, from its banks to the edges of the valley, that floods when the river runs high.

facts.text: Regular floods deposit nutrients, so floodplain soils are often very fertile.
Farms and cities have grown on floodplains to use their rich soil and fresh water, as in the Nile and Mississippi basins.
The risk of flooding has led to growing efforts to control floods.
Floodplains support diverse, productive and often very species-rich ecosystems.
Floodplain forests protect waterways from erosion and pollution and soften the impact of floodwaters.
Flood control, hydroelectric reservoirs and conversion to farmland are the main ways people destroy floodplain ecosystems.

definition.text: Most floodplains are built by rivers depositing sediment, both on the inside of their bends and when floods spill over the banks.

facts.text: A meandering river erodes the outside of each bend and deposits a point bar on the inside, building a level floodplain.
Water spilling over the banks lays down a thin layer of sediment, thickest and coarsest near the channel, forming natural levees.
In undisturbed rivers, overbank flow typically happens every one to two years.

definition.text: Floodplain ecology centres on the flood pulse: the yearly cycle of flooding and drying that brings nutrients and shapes life on the floodplain.

facts.text: Floods bring nutrient-rich debris and release nutrients from soil as it is flooded.
Many fish spawn as the flood begins, using the flooded river edge, and must grow fast before the water falls.
Floodplain plants and animals grow and die fast, letting them colonise shifting ground; floodplain trees are fast-growing.
Plant zones away from the river follow a gradient of soil moisture, oxygen and flood frequency.
Floodplain forests covered 1% of Europe in the 1800s and, less cleared than other forests, are important refuges for biodiversity.
Flood control sharpens the boundary between water and land, reducing habitat diversity.

definition.text: Floodplain flood control covers the rules, maps, insurance and works used to limit flood damage to people living on floodplains.

facts.text: River floods, especially on China's Yellow River, have been among the deadliest natural disasters, led by the 1931 China floods.
How far a floodplain floods depends on flood size, expressed as a return period such as the 100-year flood.
In the United States, the National Flood Insurance Program insures properties in flood-prone areas defined on flood risk maps.
Upstream development such as a large car park can raise flood levels, but the maps are rarely updated.
Some towns have been relocated off floodplains; elsewhere annual floods are part of the rural economy, supporting recessional agriculture.

definition.text: Floodplains can store phosphorus in their soils and plants, keeping it from overloading rivers downstream.

facts.text: Much of the phosphorus in freshwater comes from wastewater treatment plants and farm runoff, and too much is a problem.
Floodplain forests act as phosphorus sinks, and cutting rivers off from their floodplains worsens phosphorus overload.
